title: The Abnūn inscription (ŠAb), 243/4 CE — a courtier of Šābuhr I vows a fire if the Romans who came against Pārs and Pahlaw are beaten, and the Gordian III war seen from below rather than from the throne
language_note:
Middle Persian, in the Book Pahlavi transliteration convention, `pal` as persia-01-skz carries it. THE CASE DISTINCTION IN THE TRANSLITERATION IS MEANING AND NOT STYLE: capitals are ARAMAIC HETEROGRAMS — MLKAn MLKA, ZY, PWN, YHWWN, OBYDWN, YATWNd, MHYTN, ŠM — words written in Aramaic and read in Persian, and lowercase is Iranian written phonetically. Eighty-two of the main text's hundred and ten tokens carry a capital. A normalisation that lower-cased this excerpt would destroy the distinction the writing system is built on, and none has been applied.

TWO REGISTERS ARE CARRIED, BOTH SOURCE-LANGUAGE. The transliteration renders the graphemes; the NORMALISED TRANSCRIPTION renders what the editors read them as, and the transcription is where the editorial uncertainty lives — eight asterisked conjectural forms (*āšnawēn, *pāy[w]ēhēn, *nixwārān, *hēnd, *(ā)[nān] and others) and one explicit pair of alternatives, *čēr[īhād]/*čēr[bawād], where the editors cannot choose between 'were to be victorious' and 'were to become victorious'. Both registers are reproduced because dropping the transcription would drop the record of what is uncertain.
date: 243/4 CE. The text dates itself internally — QDM (Š)NT 3 šhpwhry MLKAn MLKA, 'in year 3 of Šābuhr, king of kings' — which is the war of Gordian III. THE YEAR NUMERAL IS ITSELF PARTLY UNCERTAIN in the edition: the transliteration marks the Š of (Š)NT as a doubtful reading and the transcription writes (s)āl III with the same doubt. Recorded, not resolved.

original_text_note:
Verbatim from sites.uci.edu/sasanika/abnun-inscription/, PASTED BY THE CURATOR on 2026-09-05. This session did not open the page.

EDITORIAL ACTS, DECLARED. The bracketed labels [A] and [B] and the four register headings are supplied by this record; the page presents the two inscriptions and their three registers under its own headings. The page's horizontal rules between registers are dropped. THE LINE BREAKS OF THE TRANSLITERATIONS ARE THE EDITION'S OWN and are kept, including the mid-word break `šh-\npwhry`, which is not closed up: the transliteration is set to the stone's lines and closing it would lose that. Nothing else is altered.

TWO UNBALANCED BRACKETS, ON THE PAGE AND NOT IN THE CAPTURE, LEFT AS PRINTED. The transliteration carries 13 `[` against 14 `]`: the stray one is in `[HT šh]pwhry ZY MLKA]n`, where the `]` after MLKA has no opener and the intended form is presumably MLKA[n] or [MLKA]n. The transcription carries 10 `[` against 9 `]`: the unclosed one opens at `[kū(š?) pad ban[da]gīh` and never closes. A THIRD IRREGULARITY: `pad*` in the transcription carries its asterisk AFTER the word where all seven other conjectural forms carry it before. None of the three is repaired, and none is attributed to the page rather than the paste — that would need the page open beside the paste, which is the collation this project does not perform on its own authority (FINDING 55).

WHAT DID NOT GO WRONG, MEASURED BEFORE THE RECORD WAS WRITTEN. Every diacritic in the transcription is a precomposed NFC character — ā ē ī ō ū š č ǰ — and the transliteration's ’ is U+2019 throughout, not U+0027. The heterogram case pattern is intact across all 110 tokens of the main transliteration. The `/` in *čēr[īhād]/*čēr[bawād] survives, which is the editors' alternative reading and the thing most likely to be flattened by a copy.
reference_translation:
[A] THE FOUR FIGURE-LABELS ON THE ALTAR
Ardaxšīr, king of kings
Aspēz, master of the court, Wahnām the commander
Šāpūr, king of kings
Abnūn, master of Ceremonies of the Harem

[B] THE MAIN INSCRIPTION
This fire-alter, Abnūn, the Master of Ceremonies of the Harem ordered that it should be made, and initially he said: If I am able, then I will establish this fire. Thereafter, in the year of Šābuhr, the king of kings, when the Romans came against Pārs and Pahlaw, then I was here, at Wisp-šād, at worship. After I heard the Romans were coming, then I implored the gods that if Šābuhr, the king of kings, were to be victorious, beat the Romans, and vanquish them, so that they were submissive to him, then I would hasten to establish a fire here.
and it was named Remain Šāpūr (and) Abnūn.

THE PUBLISHED ENGLISH ON THE REACHABLE PAGE IS INCOMPLETE, AND THE MISSING PART IS THE PART THIS RECORD EXISTS FOR. Between 'then I would hasten to establish a fire here.' and 'and it was named Remain Šāpūr (and) Abnūn.' the English stops, with no ellipsis and no lacuna marker, and resumes mid-sentence on a lower-case 'and'. THE MIDDLE PERSIAN CARRIES A WHOLE FURTHER MOVEMENT THERE — that the vow was fulfilled: pas kū āšnūd kū Hrōmāy āmad hēnd ud Šābuhr ī šāhān šāh zad hēnd u-š wattar kard [*hēnd tā-n pad bandagīh ēstēnd ēg-im niwist ādur-ēw] nišāyān. THE OMITTED CLAUSE IS WHERE THE ROMANS COME, ARE STRUCK BY ŠĀBUHR, AND STAND IN SERVITUDE, AND WHERE ABNŪN BEGINS THE FIRE. It is not translated on the page, and THIS RECORD DOES NOT TRANSLATE IT: a translation this project supplied itself would be worth nothing, which is the rule that killed the second reading of eastasia-05-liangshu-qin-lun. The curator checked the page and confirmed the omission is the page's and not the capture's. A reader who needs the fulfilment clause in English must go to MacKenzie or Skjærvø, neither of which is openly reachable — see citation_original.

THE READING OF THIS TEXT IS DISPUTED AMONG FIVE PUBLISHED TRANSLATIONS AND THE PAGE SAYS SO IN ITS OWN WORDS, verbatim:

"There are several major translations, first by Tavoosi; Gignoux; Livshits & Nikitin; Skjærvø; and finally by MacKenzie. It is important to note that all five translations are at times significantly different from another. We have chosen the latest translation by MacKenzie as the basis, allowing for some minor changes, along with Skjærvø’s important observations after the publication of MacKenzie. The problem with this inscription is that while these alter portray figures with their names, the inscription on fire-alter circles around it. The inscription is also grammatically problematic and tends to confuse the reader, hence the multiple interpretations and translations."

WHAT IS UNCERTAIN, AND IT IS THE WHOLE TEXT RATHER THAN A WORD IN IT. Five scholars have published translations of this inscription and the edition this record follows states that "all five translations are at times significantly different from another", and gives the reason: "The inscription is also grammatically problematic and tends to confuse the reader, hence the multiple interpretations and translations." The uncertainty is also visible in the source-language text above rather than only asserted about it: the transcription marks eight forms as conjectural with an asterisk and prints TWO ALTERNATIVE READINGS SIDE BY SIDE at *čēr[īhād]/*čēr[bawād], in the clause that says what Šābuhr was to do to the Romans.
reference_translation_note:
The English is Sasanika's own rendering, and the page states its basis: MacKenzie's translation, 'allowing for some minor changes, along with Skjærvø's important observations after the publication of MacKenzie'. IT IS THEREFORE NOT A VERBATIM REPRINT OF ANY OF THE FIVE and the published-translation test is met by citation-of-record — the same boundary F5_CANDIDATES.md recorded for this candidate before it was captured, confirmed at the page.

AND IT IS INCOMPLETE, WHICH THE HUNT DID NOT KNOW. F5_CANDIDATES.md records this candidate as having 'transliteration, normalized transcription and English translation in parallel on one open page'. That is true of the LAYOUT and false of the CONTENT: the third register stops short. Something counted three columns and did not read to the end of the third.
translation_source:
Sasanika, 'The Abnun Inscription', https://sites.uci.edu/sasanika/abnun-inscription/, rendering MacKenzie with Skjærvø's later observations.

THE FIVE EDITIONS AS THE PAGE NAMES THEM, AND IT NAMES NOTHING ELSE ABOUT THEM: 'first by Tavoosi; Gignoux; Livshits & Nikitin; Skjærvø; and finally by MacKenzie'. NO YEARS, NO JOURNALS, NO VOLUMES ARE GIVEN ON THE PAGE. F5_CANDIDATES.md supplies them — Tavoosi & Frye (BAI 3, 1989), Gignoux (Studia Iranica 20, 1991), Livshits & Nikitin (BAI n.s. 5, 1991), MacKenzie (BAI 7, 1993), Skjærvø (Studia Iranica 21, 1992) — AND THEY DID NOT COME FROM THIS PAGE. They are second-hand in this record and are recorded as such.

ONE OF THEM IS INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT WITH THE PAGE AND THE RECORD FLAGS IT RATHER THAN PICKING A SIDE. The page says its English follows MacKenzie 'along with Skjærvø's important observations AFTER THE PUBLICATION OF MacKenzie'. The hunt's citations date Skjærvø to 1992 and MacKenzie to 1993, so Skjærvø cannot both be the 1992 item and postdate MacKenzie. Either there are two Skjærvø publications or one of the years is wrong. Unresolvable from anything this project can reach: BAI 7 sits in an https-to-http redirect loop at bulletinasiainstitute.org and JSTOR stable/i24045519 is paywalled, both re-confirmed by the hunt. The page also says 'Tavoosi' where the hunt says 'Tavoosi & Frye'.

findspot: Barm-e Delak, Fārs, Iran. The fire-altar is now in the Narenjestān, Shiraz.
notes:
F5 Part 3, record 39, and F5's Persia verbatim_with_provenance slot. Persia's verbatim_machine_english slot in the same sub-tranche is recorded as a searched failure; this is the region's only F5 delivery.

WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT ROME, AND WHY IT IS WORTH MORE THAN A SECOND ROYAL INSCRIPTION. This corpus already holds the Gordian III war from the throne, in persia-01-skz, the Res Gestae Divi Saporis, where a king lists provinces and victories. THIS IS THE SAME WAR FROM UNDERNEATH. A courtier — the master of ceremonies of the harem — is at Wisp-šād at worship when he hears the Romans are coming against Pārs and Pahlaw, and he makes a private bargain with the gods: if Šābuhr beats them and they are made submissive, he will found a fire. Then he founds it, and names it after the king and after himself. Two records, one war, two social registers, and the second one is a vow rather than a claim.

GLOSS-CAPABLE, contested_reading, AND THE UNCERTAINTY IS ABOUT THE WHOLE TEXT RATHER THAN A WORD IN IT. Five published translations, named on the page, of which the page says 'all five translations are at times significantly different from another' and gives its reason — the inscription is grammatically problematic. THE MECHANICAL REQUIREMENT IS MET: the statement of uncertainty and the naming of the five editions both sit inside reference_translation, which the loader chunks, and neither is in notes, which it does not. AND THE UNCERTAINTY IS ALSO VISIBLE IN original_text_excerpt, which is unusual for this corpus: the transcription's eight asterisked conjectural forms and the side-by-side *čēr[īhād]/*čēr[bawād] are the editorial doubt shown rather than described.

THE HONEST WEAKNESS, AND IT IS THE LARGEST ON ANY RECORD IN THIS TRANCHE. THE PUBLISHED ENGLISH DOES NOT COVER THE WHOLE OF THE SOURCE TEXT. The clause in which Šābuhr strikes the Romans, they stand in servitude, and the fire is begun — the fulfilment of the vow, and the reason this record was chosen — is in the Middle Persian and is absent from the English. The slot is verbatim_with_provenance and a published translation does exist, is cited and is on the page, so the tier holds; but a reader who asks this record what happened to the Romans will find the answer only in a language the reference_translation does not reach. This record does not fill the gap itself. See reference_translation, where the omission is declared inside the chunk a reader actually meets.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO PROJECT DOCUMENTS, both from the same capture. F5_PART3_START.md's claim that Sasanika states no terms of use anywhere is false — see citation_original. And F5_CANDIDATES.md's description of the page as carrying all three registers 'in parallel' is true of the layout and false of the content. Both were fetch-side observations; both were corrected by a person opening the page. Third and fourth such corrections in this session, after the Ruwāfa page reference and the Ruwāfa licence.

WHAT WAS REJECTED FOR THIS SLOT IS RECORDED IN F5_CANDIDATES.md AND NOT RE-ARGUED HERE: Paikuli (NPi) §91, whose open text is a scan of a Reichert book on a third-party site and whose editor's own front matter is liberal with query marks on the Roman clause; and M2 I, which is a TURFAN FRAGMENT and therefore an East Asia record under this corpus's findspot rule — as is the already-banked M 5794 I, which is mis-regioned and is F6's to settle.

findspot_places.name: Barm-e Delak
findspot_places.note:
Pleiades 922623, titled 'Barm-i Dilak', feature type `monument`, locationPrecision `precise`, with an extent — confirmed present in the pinned 2026-08-10 places dump. The cited source states the findspot as Barm-e Delak in Fārs and the gazetteer holds the same monument under a variant romanisation of the same name.

ONE READING OF THE SCHEMA IS BEING MADE HERE AND IT IS FLAGGED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. PLACES.md defines `stated` as 'the record's own text names the place'. THE INSCRIPTION DOES NOT NAME ITS OWN FINDSPOT — almost no inscription does — so on the strictest reading of that sentence no findspot on any object record in this corpus could ever be `stated`, and the ground would have to be `identified` with a citation for what is really a name match, or `regional` for a place the gazetteer holds precisely. This record reads `stated` as 'the RECORD names this place, from its cited source', which is what a findspot block is for. THE TWO READINGS DIVERGE ON EVERY OBJECT RECORD IN THE CORPUS and the schema does not say which it means. Named here; not resolved here.

THE ALTAR'S CURRENT LOCATION IS NOT PLACED. It is in the Narenjestān at Shiraz, which is a museum building and not a findspot; Pleiades 922706 (Qasr-i Abu Nasr / Shiraz) resolves and is REFUSED for this block, because where an object is displayed today is neither where it was found nor where it was made and this schema has no block for it.

subject_places.name: Wisp-šād (W[s]pš’ty, Wi(s)p-šād)
subject_places.note: Where the speaker says he was — 'then I was here, at Wisp-šād, at worship' — and therefore where the vow is made and, on the reading the text supports, where the fire is founded. `focus` because the passage is organized around it: everything the text reports happens to a man standing at this place. NO GAZETTEER ENTRY: the pinned 2026-08-10 Pleiades dump was searched for wisp and for wisp-šād and returns nothing, and none has been guessed. The place-name is itself partly uncertain in the edition — the transliteration reads W[s]pš’ty with a restored s, the transcription Wi(s)p-šād with the same doubt — so a gazetteer match would be a match to a name the editors do not fully read.

subject_places.name: Pārs (p’lsy)
subject_places.note:
Named in the text as one of the two lands the Romans came against. Pleiades 922698, titled 'Persis/Pars', feature type `region`, with a real extent (roughly 51.6–53.4 E, 29.8–3x N) in the pinned dump — so this is PLACES.md's `regional`-with-an-id form drawing an extent rather than a pin, carried here on a `stated` ground because the text names it.

`mentioned`, AND THE RESTRAINT IS FORCED BY THE VOCABULARY RATHER THAN CHOSEN. The Romans MOVE INTO Pārs — that is the sentence — so this is an edge, and the roles cannot express it. A5 derives every edge as source → focus → destination, and both ends of this movement are in the text while NEITHER IS THE FOCUS: the focus is Wisp-šād, where the speaker stands. eastasia-07-tang-huiyao hit the mirror image of this and took `mentioned` for Tokharistan because one end was missing; here both ends are present and the focus is a third place. PLACES.md's 'known limit' section records that multi-leg routes flatten; THIS IS A DIFFERENT LIMIT — an edge that does not touch the focus at all — and it is recorded as an observation, not ruled on.

subject_places.name: Pahlaw (plswby)
subject_places.note: The second land the Romans came against, named beside Pārs. NO ID, AND ONE WAS FOUND AND REFUSED. Pleiades 952097 'Parthyene/Parthia' resolves in the pinned dump as a `region` with an extent at roughly 57–58 E, 38–39 N — that is Parthyene proper, and Sasanian Pahlaw in the formula Pārs ud Pahlaw denotes a considerably larger northern domain. Equating the two is a scholarly identification, which PLACES.md requires a `ground_citation` for, and the source read for this record offers none. The honest ground is `regional` with no id and the map is sparser for it. `mentioned` for the same reason as Pārs.

subject_places.name: the Romans (hlwm’dy, Hrōmāy)
subject_places.note: The text names a PEOPLE and not a city — Hrōmāy, the Romans, four times — and this record does not convert one into the other. NO ID IS TAKEN, and specifically Pleiades 423025 Roma is NOT imported here: arabia-06-syllaeus carries 423025 because its Safaitic text says rm, the place, where this text says the Romans, the people. The two records now hold the same adversary under two grounds and the difference is in the sources, not in the editing. The corpus has a precedent for placing a people without an id — eastasia-07-tang-huiyao's Dashi — and one for placing a people WITH an id, arabia-05-ruwafa's Thamudaei at Pleiades 814740, which was taken only because Pleiades holds that ethnonym as a place with an extent. Nothing in the pinned dump does the same for the Romans as a people.
